grand_strategy.reading:
Albania runs the strategy of a small state that has bet everything on being
the most useful and best-aligned partner of whoever matters, and on Edi Rama
as the man who makes that bet personal. Every relation in the card follows
from it: NATO and the American channel for security, the EU for the future,
Italy and the UK for the migration currency, the Gulf and the Kushners for
capital, Turkey for arms and religion, Kosovo for the nation. The Luttwak
pattern is that each source of leverage creates a counter-pressure that
lands on the same pillar. The EU path is only as fast as the rule of law
allows, which is the front where Rama fights his own prosecutors; the
Kosovo pact adds to Albania's security and to Serbia's rearmament; the
Trump channel brings the Board of Peace and the Sazan protests together.
In 2026 the EU front is moving (three chapters closed on 14 Jul, the
Commission calling Albania and Montenegro the closest candidates) while the
American front is cooling (the 2027 NATO summit dropped from the draft
text, 10% tariffs). Two signals that are not rows: Albania's own ministers
played down the US embassy's Iran warning of 1 Apr 2026, and Greek
diplomatic sources publicly distanced Athens from Rama's claim at Delphi
that a Hague referral was agreed. The test is whether the EU path survives
the collision between Rama's immunities draft and the benchmarks, with
Greece as a possible veto at the end.

grand_strategy.reading:
Bosnia and Herzegovina has no single grand strategy, and a card that pretends it
has one would be wrong. The objectives above are those of the state-level
institutions as the Bosniak-led majority reads them: the Presidency member
Becirovic, the foreign minister Konakovic, the Constitutional and State Courts,
the Central Election Commission, the SDA/SDP/Troika parties. Two other agendas
sit inside the same state. The Republika Srpska leadership of Dodik's SNSD,
which has just won again, wants to hollow the state out - competences back to
the entity, the OHR gone, status defined in Washington and Moscow - and keeps
the Serb seat in the Presidency (Cvijanovic) to veto what it cannot win. The
HDZ BiH leadership of Covic, backed by Zagreb, wants an election law that stops
non-Croats from choosing the Croat member and has just obtained the seat
outright. The paradox of the whole card is that a state must defend its
existence against one of its own entities, with tools (the Bonn powers, EUFOR,
Security Council cover, the courts) that belong in part to others, in a year in
which the guarantors weakened - Schmidt resigned in May and no successor was
agreed by mid-July, the US lifted its sanctions and said it was done with
nation-building, Orban fell in April - while the electorate stayed home (42%).
Signals that are not rows: the 31 Oct 2026 Security Council vote on EUFOR (the
October 2025 renewal was 15-0, so the base case is renewal; Russia's line on the
OHR is the thing to watch), the identity of the next High Representative,
whether Hungary under Magyar keeps Orban's line toward Banja Luka, and whether
the new Presidency can still produce a majority on foreign-policy questions
after Komsic's seat goes to HDZ. Sarajevo's room for manoeuvre is real only
where the EU and the entity cannot veto it: the courts, memory politics and the
capacity to say no to Belgrade.

Zagreb denies an arms race but reads Serbian rearmament (Chinese CM-400AKG missiles confirmed in March 2026) as a risk to report to the Alliance.

grand_strategy.reading:
Croatia plays the strategy of a small state that has solved its existential
question - NATO and the EU - and is now spending the dividend. Its first
objective is no longer to be admitted but to make Serbia's rearmament and
its own memory politics the neighbour's problem: it deters from inside the
Alliance, speaks to Belgrade in the voice of a member state (conditionality
on the missing, a reported weapons purchase, a defence declaration with
Tirana and Pristina) and keeps the instruments that are not its own - the
US licence on JANAF, EU loans for tanks, the High Representative in
Sarajevo - within reach. The Luttwakian pattern is that every lever is
borrowed and every success invites the response it was meant to prevent:
deterrence feeds Serbian rearmament, a refusal to receive Vucic hands him
the memorial stage, discipline on Russian oil prices out a Hungarian
partner it needs for INA. Domestically the strategy has two authors:
Plenkovic, EU-centred, tied to a Homeland Movement coalition, and
Milanovic, re-elected with 74.9%, who vetoes deployments and cancels
summits; Belgrade reads the harder voice. Two signals that are not
rows: Orban's fall in April 2026 has changed the weather with Hungary
overnight, and Serbia's snap election of 25 October 2026 may reset a tone
that Zagreb has so far refused to reset. Bosnia, where Zagreb's kin are
a constituent people dependent on imposed rules, is the arena in which
its soft power is thinnest.

grand_strategy.reading:
North Macedonia runs the strategy of a state that has already paid for entry
twice and now treats a third payment as a trap. It changed its name for NATO
(2018-20), accepted the French proposal for the EU (2022), and still has no date;
the Mickoski government, in office since June 2024 after winning 58 of 120 seats, draws the
conclusion that every concession reopens the account, and trades speed for
guarantees. The result is the Luttwakian pattern of a weak actor playing a long
game against two veto-holders: it keeps the one thing it has already won (NATO,
near-total alignment with Brussels on Russia and Ukraine) and widens its list of
patrons, with Washington, Ankara and, until Orban's fall, Budapest and Belgrade
behind it. The price is a country neither inside nor outside the EU, and a
population that votes with its feet. Two signals that are not rows: the
Commission's report of November 2025 states flatly that 'no attempts were made' to
adopt the amendments, while von der Leyen's visit of 2 October 2026 produced the
first agreed step in years, so the next weeks (the foreign minister's trip to Sofia
during a Corridor 8 event) are the test of whether the 'stronger pressure' Mickoski
awaits has arrived. Open gaps: no source was found on Russian influence on the
2024 vote, on Chinese projects under this government, or on any Greek retaliation
after 2024.

grand_strategy.reading: Montenegro runs the grand strategy of a twenty-year-old micro-state that has bet its survival on being absorbed into the institutions that guarantee small states: NATO (done in 2017) and the EU (the 2028 target). The method is alignment as proof - full CFSP alignment, expulsions of Russian operatives, a defence budget above 2% - and the resource is speed: it is the only candidate with 18 chapters closed. The Luttwakian trap is that the last chapters are not technical. Croatia's veto turns on wartime grievances from the 1990s, and the Spajic majority rests on parties that treat the 2006 independence as a wound, so every step that pleases Belgrade's friends at home (the Jasenovac resolution, the Mladic condolences) costs a vote in Zagreb or The Hague, while every step toward Brussels costs the coalition's Serbian flank. The same logic runs through the economy: the Gulf and Turkish capital that replaces Chinese debt arrives with procedure-bypassing laws that the Commission itself flags. Two signals that are not rows: the cadence of closures (December 2025, January, March, June and July 2026) and President Milatovic's repeated returns of laws to Parliament, a veto that keeps the Constitutional Court and Brussels in the loop. With the Serbian election on 25 Oct 2026 and Montenegro's own on June 2027, the question is whether the accession treaty can be finished before the identity politics of one of the two neighbours changes the arithmetic.

grand_strategy.reading:
Serbia runs a hedging strategy with one fixed point - Kosovo - and everything else
negotiable. In Luttwak's terms the paradox is structural: the instrument that
protects the fixed point (Russian and Chinese cover at the UN) is the one that
blocks the declared strategic goal (EU membership), and the "neutrality" that
justifies the hedge is financed by the side the hedge is meant to keep at a
distance. Through 2025-26 the hedge stopped paying: the US sanctioned NIS, Russia
refused a long-term gas contract and accused Belgrade over ammunition, the EU
froze funds and talks after the Mladić funeral. Two signals worth watching that
are not rows: Vučić did not attend the 2026 Moscow parade, and in May 2026 Serbia
held its first-ever exercise with NATO on its own soil. The 25 Oct 2026 election
decides whether the strategy has an author at all.

grand_strategy.reading:
Kosovo runs the strategy of a state that exists on the ground and not yet in
law: every move is a bid to turn effective control into recognised status, and
the only currencies it has are loyalty and usefulness to the West. That
produces the central Luttwakian pattern: the actions that prove statehood
(mayors in the north, the army, rail stations, the war-memory law) are the
ones that cost it the patrons who could confer it, while the actions that would
please the patrons (the Community of Serb-majority Municipalities, Serbian
return to the judiciary) are those it fears would hollow out statehood from
within. Since 2025 the pressure has eased on one flank (EU measures lifted in
March 2026, institutions completed in September-October) and tightened on
another (KFOR shrinking, a cooler Washington, the Specialist Chambers
verdicts). Two signals that are not rows: the US launched a strategic dialogue with
Belgrade on 17 July 2026 although Kosovo had joined the Board of Peace and
pledged troops to Gaza, and the 6 Oct law on the Hague court was passed under
street pressure, not diplomatic calculation. With
the 25 Oct Serbian election ahead, Pristina's real question is whether the
stalled Ohrid road can be re-opened by a new government in Belgrade.

Partner, not ally: no bilateral alliance, and the Mickoski government has a recurring friction with Tirana-adjacent politics - students and politicians from Albania and Kosovo joined the April-May 2026 bar-exam protests, DUI's Trajanov called that 'impermissible external influence', and Albania left the cross-border programme without a Joint Technical Secretariat in July 2024 (Commission). Grade C because no source calls the state-to-state relation by name; the stance is the structural reading. Bond - kin: language and ethnicity of a large part of the electorate, a standing tie.

Orban lost the April 2026 election: Prime Minister Magyar called Gruevski 'a criminal', and on 1 Sep 2026 Hungarian police opened a criminal probe into Eximbank deals including the Skopje loan. Partner, not ally, although both are NATO members; the opposition calls Orban and Vucic Mickoski's mentors. Trend cooling because the personal patron has gone and the loan is under investigation. Bond - affinity: a shared conservative-nationalist camp, which survived the fall of its leader only as a debt.

Rival, not adversary: Skopje wants no confrontation beyond NATO and EU alignment, and the Mickoski government has been quiet. Confidence C because no source in the pool uses 'rival' and nothing recent (2025-26) was found; an alleged Russian influence on the 2024 vote is not sourced. MNE.note: Mirrors Serbia's own stance toward Montenegro (SRB: rival, kin; Boll Belgrade, 28 May 2026: Montenegro an 'alienated part of Serbian space', a 'doctrine of limited sovereignty'; 2023 census 32.93% Serbs). Seen from Podgorica: Vucic's 14 May 2026 'secession' remarks drew a Foreign Ministry reply that Montenegro 'neither seceded from Serbia nor was ever part of it'; in early June 2026 police banned 87 men flown from Belgrade before the Tivat summit and called it 'hybrid activity'; in August Spajic spoke of coordinated hybrid action by two regional states (media read it as Albania and Serbia, a reading the government itself walked back for Albania). Not 'adversary': Serbia recognised Montenegro within days of the 2006 referendum, is its largest trade partner (17% of imports, 27% of exports) and the largest tourist market, and the government keeps a language of good neighbourliness. Cooling because 2026 added three public clashes to an unresolved dual-citizenship and language agenda. Bond - kin: a third of Montenegro's own citizens declare as Serbs and the Serbian Orthodox Church is the only canonical Orthodox church there (as in Serbia's own stance note); the grade is our structural reading of competing interests, supported by the Boll essay and the 2026 exchanges.

Not a treaty ally in the Article 42(7) sense (Montenegro is a candidate), but a stable de facto alignment that the ontology's 'ally' grade covers: 'full and resolute' CFSP alignment praised by the European Parliament on 17 Jun 2026, euro in use since 2002, 18 of 33 chapters provisionally closed by 14 Jul 2026, EU leaders' summit in Tivat on 5 Jun 2026 where von der Leyen called accession 'within reach'. Warming because of the pace of closures and the Growth Plan (EUR 89.3m released by May 2026); the Croatian veto, the Mladic condolences and the UAE procurement exemption are frictions inside the alignment, not changes in structure. Bond - affinity: a stated strategic goal, not kinship.

MNE.note: Review 2026-10-12: regraded reluctant_ally - co-members of NATO/EU with visible friction are allies by necessity, not rivals (ONTOLOGY scale). NATO and EU-candidacy partner on paper, but Croatia is the one EU member that holds a veto on the last chapters and is using it: persona non grata for Speaker Mandic, MP Knezevic and Deputy PM Becic (July 2024, after the Jasenovac resolution); Chapter 31 blocked since December 2024, Chapter 14 and others held on 22 Sep 2026 and the 22 Sep intergovernmental conference cancelled; the 22 Jul 2026 list of demands (Morinj camp compensation, 14 missing, the ship Jadran, maritime border, a swimming-pool name); 'unacceptable' on Mandic's Mladic condolences. Co-membership of NATO would derive an 'ally' stance; the hand-written grade replaces it because on the one objective that matters most (EU entry) Zagreb is the principal obstacle. 'Rival', not 'adversary': Croatia wants the issues settled, not Montenegro defeated. Bond - grievance: the 1991-92 Morinj camp, the Prevlaka and Jadran disputes, and the 2024 Jasenovac resolution.

SRB.note: Strategic dialogue launched in Washington on 17 July 2026; Vučić told Fox News relations were 'dramatically transformed'. Documented friction over NIS sanctions, tariffs and Kosovo. Bond - grievance: the 1999 NATO bombing and the 2008 recognition of Kosovo; about half of Serbians regard the US as an enemy (poll via N1). Structural check: Washington is also Pristina's de facto guarantor (KFOR, Javelins, Board of Peace charter of Jan 2026, see XKX); Belgrade's 'partner' grade rests on transactional gains (strategic dialogue, NIS licences) and on the Trump administration's perceived softness on Kosovo (Vučić, N1, March 2026), not on any shared position on Kosovo.

Transactional cooperation continues (Open Balkan; joint Vučić-Rama op-ed on EU accession, Feb 2026) and Vučić calls Albania a 'reliable partner' - recorded as what the government says, not as the grade. XKX.note: Pristina's aim is recognition and normalisation (it signed the Brussels Basic Agreement and the Ohrid annex in 2023), not Serbia's defeat or the end of its regime, so the ontology's 'adversary' (mortal enemy) does not apply; Serbia, by contrast, denies Kosovo's existence. Friction is sharp - Banjska (3 life/30-year sentences on 24 Apr 2026, Radoicic still at large in Serbia), the Kosovo foreign ministry's description of Belgrade's reaction to the March 2025 defence declaration as 'aggressive and threatening', the trade ban of 2023-24. No source uses the word 'rival': the grade is our reading of the structure (confidence C). Bond - grievance: the 1998-99 war and Serbia's refusal to recognise.

XKX.note: No bilateral treaty of alliance, but stable de facto alignment: the 18 Mar 2025 trilateral defence declaration with Croatia, 13 agreements signed in July 2023, Rama in Pristina on 16 Feb 2026, the Albanian free-trade area since 2003. Friction is real (Rama cancelled the 2023 joint government meeting over format; of 86 agreements about half are implemented) but nothing that changes the structure. Bond - kin: language, ethnicity; Tirana is Pristina's motherland. Belgrade reads this alignment as the 'greatest threat', so the asymmetric pair SRB-ALB is deliberate.

Cooling because Washington now seems to hedge: it wants UNMIK closed (SCR), is reviewing its KFOR contingent, and launched a strategic dialogue with Serbia on 17 Jul 2026; a 2026 Koha analysis says Serbia read Washington better than Kosovo did. Bond - affinity: Pristina's founding narrative of US support (Osmani: 'American support has been and remains vital').

XKX.note: Stabilisation and Association Agreement in force since April 2016, visa-free travel since 1 Jan 2024, full voluntary alignment with CFSP, membership application of Dec 2022 - but the EU is not an ally (no guarantee) and five members do not recognise Kosovo. Warming because all 2023 punitive measures were lifted by March 2026 (the Commission said it would 'fully re-engage'); the European Parliament in June 2026 asked for candidate status once criteria are met. France and Italy had resisted lifting the measures earlier. Bond - affinity: a stated strategic goal, not kinship.

XKX.note: Stable de facto alignment but no formal tie: no Article 5, no Partnership for Peace (four NATO members do not recognise Kosovo), only the KFOR mandate under UNSCR 1244 and an associate seat in the NATO Parliamentary Assembly. Cooling because NATO announced on 12 Jun 2026 a reduction from 4,739 to 3,000-3,500 troops (reversible). Pristina's declared goal is membership (parliamentary resolution of 3 Mar 2022). Bond - affinity: dependence on KFOR since 1999, shared lines with the West.

XKX.note: Free-trade agreement in force since 2019, bilateral trade of about USD 750m-1bn, TB2 drones and a military-financial cooperation agreement, Erdogan-Kurti meeting at the UN on 21 Sep 2026. Friction: Erdogan has told Kurti that Turkey expects progress in reducing tensions with Belgrade, and KFOR objected to the drone purchase. Bond - affinity: Ottoman heritage and a shared Muslim community; no kinship.

Bond - affinity: shared reading of Serbia and the Yugoslav wars, not kinship.

Berlin is a Quint power that presses Pristina on the Association of Serb municipalities. Bond - affinity through the diaspora, not kinship.

XKX.note: The UK backs Kosovo's Euro-Atlantic path, pressed Serbia over Banjska and at the UN Security Council in April 2026 urged non-recognisers to recognise; Kosovo's government calls it 'one of its closest allies' (Davos meeting with Powell, Jan 2026). The ambassador called 2025 a 'wasted year' and demands the Association of Serb Municipalities in 2026, and London has asked for a UNMIK review. Partner rather than ally: no security guarantee beyond KFOR.

XKX.note: Russia does not recognise Kosovo, calls it an 'inseparable part of Serbia' (Zakharova, March 2026) and blocks the UN seat; Kosovo applies all sanctions packages on Russia and Belarus. Pristina does not seek Russia's defeat, so not 'adversary'. Kurti in 2022: 'Belgrade and the Kremlin should think twice' about acting against Kosovo. Bond - grievance: Moscow's veto on Kosovo's existence and its patronage of Belgrade.

XKX.note: China has no diplomatic relations with Pristina, backs Serbia's territorial integrity at the UN (Vucic in Beijing, Sep 2025) and holds a veto on the UN seat; Chinese goods lead Kosovo's imports, so the relation is politically closed and economically open. Pristina does not campaign against Beijing; the 'rival' grade is the structural reading of competing interests, not a Kosovar statement (confidence C). Possible Taiwan-analogy fear in Beijing.

XKX.note: Montenegro recognised Kosovo in 2008 (49th state), supported its Council of Europe bid in the Committee of Ministers, and its ambassador met Kurti on 2026-02. Podgorica says its support is 'not directed against Serbia', and it avoids a stance that reads as directed against Belgrade, so it stays at partner. Bond none: Montenegro has Serbian-Orthodox kin ties to Belgrade, not to Pristina.

XKX.note: Recognised in 2008, diplomatic relations since 2009; Skopje voted for Kosovo's Council of Europe bid in 2023, contributes to KFOR (thanked by Kurti, Aug 2024), and the two governments signed agreements on education, energy and movement (Nov 2024) and discussed shared border points (Jul 2025). Skopje's own EU path and its Albanian minority keep it close but not aligned.

XKX.note: Bosnia and Herzegovina is a non-recogniser: in 2020 the Bosniak and Croat Presidency members backed recognition but the Serb member refused and Republika Srpska invoked a vital-interest veto. Bosnia has no veto over Kosovo's EU or Council of Europe path, so Pristina's posture is neutral rather than rival; the latest evidence found is from 2020 (confidence C). The Free Trade Agreement in CEFTA ties the two economies.

sources.title: Dodik to initiate mechanism to veto Bosnia's recognition of Kosovo

XKX.note: Republika Srpska is the lever that keeps Bosnia a non-recogniser: Dodik declared that recognising Kosovo would open the question of RS's own status and that RS and Kosovo 'want the same thing - independence' (2020). Belgrade backs RS (SRB: ally, kin). No Kosovar statement about RS was found; the grade is the structural reading (confidence C), and the 'partner of an adversary's ally' logic is not triggered because Pristina has no tie to RS.

XKX.note: Spain is one of the five EU non-recognisers that block candidate status, and its ambassador in Belgrade repeated that it defends Serbia's territorial integrity. Madrid supports the EU dialogue, takes part in EU-Western Balkans summits, and says it could follow if normalisation includes mutual recognition. The 'rival' grade is the structural block, not hostility (confidence C): Pristina's stated goal depends on Spanish consent.

relations.summary: Hour-long Vučić-Putin call on gas, NIS and Ukraine; gas deal extended to 31 Dec 2026 at EUR 318 per 1,000 m3; Vučić announced his resignation the next day.

Srbijagas CEO Bajatović: gas supply deal with Russia extended through end of year

sources.title: Belgrade recalls ambassador from Zagreb

relations.summary: Ratko Mladić buried in Belgrade with an army honour guard, five ministers and the Russian ambassador present; the EU cancelled Commissioner Kos's visit and called the funeral 'shocking'.

relations.summary: Pristina seeks Serbia's recognition, or at least de facto acceptance of Kosovo's statehood, as the end of the EU-facilitated normalisation; Vucic says recognition 'will not happen'. Recognition tallies are contested.

claims.text: about 120 states recognise Kosovo, about 20 recognitions reconfirmed and 4 new (Osmani, Jan 2026)

sources.title: Vucic: no one should hope for recognition of Kosovo by Serbia, that will not happen
Kosovo - October 2026 monthly forecast

relations.summary: Kosovo is not a member of the United Nations; a seat is blocked in the Security Council by Russia and China, which do not recognise it and back Serbia's territorial integrity. 110 UN members are cited by Wikipedia's index; Pristina counts about 120.

sources.title: Kosovo - October 2026 monthly forecast (Council dynamics)

relations.summary: Membership application filed 15 Dec 2022; the European Parliament (17 Jun 2026) asks the Council to move toward candidate status once the criteria are met. Five EU members do not recognise Kosovo.

sources.title: 2025 Commission report on Kosovo - European Parliament resolution (procedure 2025/2252(INI))
Spain's impact on Kosovo's accession process into the EU

relations.summary: Parliament called on the government to start NATO accession on 3 Mar 2022; the working group seeks Partnership for Peace first. Four NATO members do not recognise Kosovo.

Ukrainian crisis has revived Kosovo's long-standing aspirations for NATO membership

relations.summary: Application filed 12 May 2022; PACE gave a positive opinion (Opinion 302, April 2024) but the Committee of Ministers has not admitted Kosovo, with Serbia opposing despite Article 4 of the Ohrid annex; in June 2026 PACE was again asked to deplore Serbia's opposition.

sources.title: PACE amendment deploring that Serbia still opposes Kosovo's accession
sources.publisher: Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe

sources.title: Wider Europe briefing - Kosovo could finally get into the Council of Europe

relations.summary: Spain, one of five EU non-recognisers, repeats that it does not recognise Kosovo while backing the EU dialogue; its position is read as tied to Catalonia and the Basque Country.

sources.title: Spain's impact on Kosovo's accession process into the EU

relations.summary: Brussels Agreement on the path to normalisation (27 Feb 2023) and Ohrid implementation annex (18 Mar 2023). Kosovo has not formed the Community of Serb-majority Municipalities or sent its statute to the Constitutional Court; Serbia has not honoured Article 4 (no objection to Kosovo's memberships). Kallas on 22 Sep 2026 reaffirmed both as binding.

sources.title: Kosovo - October 2026 monthly forecast
The NGO Aktiv report - the Ohrid Agreement and regional integration

relations.summary: Trilateral declaration on military cooperation with Albania and Croatia (Tirana, 18 Mar 2025); 13 agreements and declarations signed by the two governments on 6 Jul 2023. A declaration of intent, not an alliance treaty.

sources.title: A Front against Serbia?
Albania, Croatia and Kosovo sign defense agreement - a new military alliance in the Balkans

relations.summary: Co-signatory of the 18 Mar 2025 trilateral declaration on military cooperation (Tirana); Bulgaria was invited to join. Serbia called it an 'arms race'.

Vucic: Albania and Croatia have started an arms race after the memorandum with Kosovo

relations.summary: Stabilisation and Association Agreement in force since April 2016; visa-free travel to the Schengen area since 1 Jan 2024; voluntary alignment with CFSP including restrictive measures on Russia and Belarus. Not a candidate.

sources.title: 2025 Commission report on Kosovo - European Parliament resolution (procedure 2025/2252(INI))

relations.summary: Charter of Trump's Board of Peace signed as a founding member at Davos on 22 Jan 2026 (Osmani); the charter does not oblige members to send troops. Earlier: Washington Agreement on economic normalisation with Serbia (4 Sep 2020, with an exchange of recognition with Israel).

sources.title: Kosovo invited to join Trump's Board of Peace

sources.publisher: Office of the Prime Minister of Kosovo

relations.summary: KFOR numbered 4,739 troops from 31 nations in June 2026; NATO announced on 12 Jun a gradual reduction toward 3,000-3,500 over the next year, reversible. KFOR is the actual shield and controls Kosovo's airspace under UNSCR 1244.

sources.title: KFOR Placemat, June 2026

relations.summary: Just under 600 US troops in KFOR (April 2026 figures); a US EUCOM official said Washington would adjust its contribution after the NATO review.

sources.title: NATO to cut Kosovo peacekeeper numbers

relations.summary: 246 Javelin FGM-148F missiles with tracking equipment approved by DSCA on 11 Jan 2024 (about EUR 69m, USD 75m), the core of the Kosovo Security Force's anti-armour capability.

sources.title: Kosovo to receive weapons from the US as part of military development plan

relations.summary: The diaspora (nearly 600,000 people in Germany; Germany and Switzerland together supply about three quarters of remittances) sent EUR 1.35bn in 2024 (13% of GDP by OECD) and EUR 1.4bn in 2025.

relations.summary: Measures imposed on Kosovo by the EU in June 2023 over tensions in the northern municipalities (funds suspended, high-level contacts frozen). The EU announced the lifting on 17 Dec 2025 and the Commission confirmed on 17 Mar 2026 that all had been lifted and all frozen assistance released.

sources.title: Kosovo leaders welcome lifting of all EU punitive measures
The EU is lifting all punitive measures

relations.summary: Banjska attack (24 Sep 2023): armed Serbs killed police sergeant Afrim Bunjaku; three gunmen died. Milan Radoicic, who admitted organising it, lives in Serbia.

sources.title: Kosovo court jails three Serb separatists over 2023 Banjska attack

relations.summary: Pristina Basic Court sentenced Blagoje Spasojevic and Vladimir Tolic to life and Dusan Maksimovic to 30 years for Banjska (24 Apr 2026, first instance); the court refused a trial in absentia for Radoicic and 40 others. Serbia called the verdict 'draconian' and 'politically motivated'.

sources.title: Kosovo court hands life sentences over deadly Banjska attack
A first-instance verdict

relations.summary: Ban on Serbian goods introduced in mid-2023; on 7 Oct 2024 eased at the Merdare crossing under inspection, with other crossings staying closed until scanners are installed. EU and US welcomed the decision.

sources.title: Kosovo lifts import ban on Serbian goods at Merdare border crossing

relations.summary: In the 12 Oct 2025 local elections the Serb List won all four northern municipalities (Zvecan, Leposavic, Zubin Potok, North Mitrovica) and returned to the institutions after 928 days; its vote share fell by 11.4 points on average.

sources.title: Serb List returns to power in north Kosovo after 928 days outside institutions
Serb List dominates local elections but sees decline in support

relations.summary: Kosovo police arrested seven directors of Serbia-run institutions in Gracanica (19 May 2026) and took control of four Serbia-operated railway stations in the north (28 May 2026); in July-September 2026 the judicial councils dismissed 7 prosecutors and 18 judges who sought to return after the 2022 Serb walk-out.

sources.title: Kosovo - October 2026 monthly forecast

relations.summary: NATO announced on 12 Jun 2026 a gradual KFOR reduction toward 3,000-3,500 troops (back to 2023 levels), reversible and coordinated with troop rotations; KFOR will keep supporting the EU-led dialogue.

sources.title: NATO to cut troop numbers in Kosovo amid improved security situation
KFOR Placemat, June 2026

relations.summary: Kosovo imposed its own sanctions on Russia in 2022 (asset freezes, access to markets) and has since aligned with EU packages on Russia and Belarus; Kurti said it had applied 13 packages. Kosovo is not a UN member and takes no UN votes.

relations.summary: Kosovo announced its first military aid to Ukraine on 20 Mar 2024 (armoured vehicles, trucks and mortar rounds), despite Ukraine not recognising Kosovo; it has also trained Ukrainian deminers.

sources.title: Kosovo announces its first-ever military aid packages for Ukraine

relations.summary: Kosovo's parliament approved on 30 Mar 2026 sending troops to the International Stabilisation Force in Gaza under Trump's Board of Peace (pledge announced in February); the contribution is to be negotiated and approved case by case.

sources.title: Kosovo approves troops to Gaza under US-backed scheme
Kosovo has committed to send Kosovo Security Force members to Gaza

relations.summary: Kosovo announced in July 2023 the purchase of Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones; KFOR said the purchase conflicted with its authority over Kosovo's airspace. Turkey has supported the KSF transformation since 2018 (equipment, training, an ammunition agreement).

sources.title: Kosovo buys Turkish Bayraktar drones
Turkish arming of Kosovo: continuation of military cooperation or Ankara's support for Kurti?

relations.summary: Erdogan received Kurti in a closed-door meeting at the UN General Assembly sidelines in New York on 21 Sep 2026, covering bilateral ties and the region.

sources.title: Turkiye's President meets Kosovar premier at UN sidelines

issues.title: Taiwan
issues.subtitle: who recognises the Republic of China
issues.why: Twelve governments keep formal ties with Taipei; everyone else has chosen Beijing. The list shrinks every few years.

issues.title: Palestine
issues.subtitle: who recognises the State of Palestine
issues.why: The 2024-25 wave of Western recognitions moved the line that had stood since 1988.

issues.title: Kosovo
issues.subtitle: who recognises it
issues.why: Recognition is Serbia's and Kosovo's whole contest; five EU members still refuse, Belgrade campaigns for withdrawals.

issues.title: Ukraine
issues.subtitle: the last General Assembly vote on the war
issues.why: The February 2026 vote, with the United States abstaining, shows where the coalition stands four years in.

issues.title: Ukraine, March 2022
issues.subtitle: the first vote on the aggression
issues.why: The baseline - 141 in favour - against which every later vote on Ukraine is read.

issues.title: Annexations
issues.subtitle: the October 2022 vote on Russia's annexation of Ukrainian regions
issues.why: Territorial integrity is the one principle almost every state will vote for, even those close to Moscow.

issues.title: Srebrenica
issues.subtitle: the 2024 genocide remembrance vote
issues.why: Serbia campaigned against it and counted the 68 abstentions as a victory; the vote maps the Balkans' memory wars onto the world.

issues.title: Gaza
issues.subtitle: the 2024 vote to end Israel's presence in the territories
issues.why: The clearest line of the Gaza war in the Assembly, with the West split in three.

issues.title: Palestine at the UN
issues.subtitle: the September 2026 vote on Palestine's participation
issues.why: After the recognitions, the procedural vote that measures them.
